unit.title: Interpret electrical standard, specifications and manuals

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which document sets out the rules for electrical installations that are law and must be met?
options: The maker's sales brochure for the cable
The client's colour scheme for the rooms
A trainee's notes from an earlier job
The electrical code or regulations

questions.stem: What is a job specification?
options: A list of tools that each trainee must bring to work
The client's details of the materials and work wanted
The maker's guide to using one product safely in the home
A record of the hours each worker spends on the job

questions.stem: What is a maker's installation manual mainly for?
options: To show how to install, use and maintain that product
To show the price of that product in each of the shops
To list the names of the people who designed it
To advertise other products from the same maker

questions.stem: Which document gives the hazards, safe handling and first aid for a chemical such as PVC pipe cement?
options: The job's lighting layout drawing
The cement tin's price label
The chemical's safety data sheet
The site's daily attendance list

questions.stem: What is a standard, such as a national standard for cables?
options: A price list that every seller must charge
A drawing of one building's wiring layout
An agreed set of rules for making or testing things
A letter from the client asking for some extra work to be done

questions.stem: Which document gives the ratings, sizes and other technical figures of one product, usually on one or two pages?
options: The product's data sheet
The site's daily diary
The job's final invoice
The supplier's delivery note

questions.stem: What does an electrical layout drawing usually show?
options: How each component works inside
The price of each item to be fitted
The working hours of the electricians
Where lights, switches and sockets go

questions.stem: You need every page about earthing in a 400-page manual. Where is the quickest place to look?
options: The front cover
The index at the back
The first chapter only
The warranty card

questions.stem: What does the table of contents at the front of a manual show?
options: The chapters and sections, with page numbers
The words used in the manual and what they mean
The names of the people who wrote each chapter
The list of products the maker has for sale

questions.stem: A heading in a manual reads '5.3 Earthing connections'. What does '5.3' tell you?
options: It is on page 53 of the manual
It is the third manual in a set of five
It is section 3 of chapter 5
It applies to 5.3 mm² earth cable

questions.stem: How can you check that the standard or manual you are using is the latest one?
options: Check that its cover is clean and none of it is torn
Check that it has the most pages of any copy
Check that it was printed in the same colour
Check its edition or revision date is current

questions.stem: A note on a drawing says 'See detail B, sheet 4'. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as notes are only there for the designer
Look at detail B on sheet 4 for more information
Fit four of item B wherever the note is placed
Ask the client to draw detail B for you on site

questions.stem: What does the signal word CAUTION on a safety label usually warn about?
options: A hazard that will kill you or injure you very badly
A note about looking after the equipment
A hazard that may cause minor or moderate injury
A reminder to read the maker's warranty card

questions.stem: A manual says the equipment works on '220 V ± 10 %'. What is the lowest supply voltage it is meant to work on?
On a drawing, what do the letters NTS mean?
options: New technical standard
Not to scale
Neutral to switch
No test supply

questions.stem: A heater is rated 1.5 kW. How many watts is this?
On a drawing, a detail is marked 'TYP' (typical). What does this usually mean?
options: The same detail is used at every similar place
The detail must be typed up again by the office staff
The detail is only a type of rough sketch
The detail is used at that one place only

questions.stem: A motor nameplate shows a power of 4 kW. What does this figure tell you?
options: The power it takes from the supply when starting
The power used by its cooling fan on its own
The power it gives out at its shaft at full load
The power it uses when it is running with no load

questions.stem: What is the 'rated current' shown on a nameplate?
options: The current it draws for a moment when first switched on
The current it draws at full load and rated voltage
The largest current its cable can ever carry
The current at which its own fuse will blow

questions.stem: A light fitting is marked IP65. What does the first digit, 6, tell you?
options: It is protected against strong water jets
It can be put under water for up to 6 hours
It is rated to carry a current of 6 amps
It is dust-tight, so no dust can get in

questions.stem: Which IP rating is the best choice for an outdoor light fitting that will be exposed to rain and dust?
options: IP65
IP20
IP10
IP00

questions.stem: What does the insulation class letter (such as F) on a motor nameplate tell you?
options: The number of wires in the motor's cable
The type of fixing the motor's feet need
The safe top temperature of the windings
The grade of paint used on the motor's body

questions.stem: A water pump's nameplate says '220 V'. The supply at the point where it will be fitted is 110 V. What should you do?
options: Connect it, as it will just run more slowly
Do not connect it; report the mismatch
Connect it, and change the fuse to a larger one
Connect it to the 110 V supply and test it

questions.stem: A motor nameplate shows two voltages, such as '230/400 V'. What does this mean?
options: It needs both supplies at the same time to run
It runs at 230 V for half the day, then 400 V
It must always be fed with 630 V in total
It can be linked for either supply voltage

questions.stem: Where should you look for the correct way to link a motor's terminals for the supply?
options: The connection diagram in the terminal box or manual
The colour of the motor's paint and the size of its feet
The sales leaflet that came with the motor
The guess of the person who delivered it

questions.stem: A maker's table gives these ratings for one installation method: 1.5 mm² – 16 A, 2.5 mm² – 21 A, 4 mm² – 28 A, 6 mm² – 36 A. A circuit must carry 24 A. What is the smallest cable from this table that may be used?
options: 1.5 mm²
2.5 mm²
4 mm²
6 mm²

questions.stem: A cable table gives ratings at a set air temperature. If the cable runs through a hot roof space, what happens to the current it can safely carry?
options: It goes up, because the heat helps the current flow
It goes down, as the cable cannot cool as well
It stays the same, as heat has no effect
It doubles, as long as the cable is new

questions.stem: Why must the current rating of a cable be reduced when many cables are bunched tightly together?
options: The cables can easily be pulled out of the bunch
The cables will rub and change colour
The cables will pick up radio signals
The cables cannot get rid of their heat well

questions.stem: A maker's manual gives the clear space needed round an inverter: top 300 mm, sides 150 mm, front 600 mm. How much space must be left at each side?
options: 150 mm
300 mm
600 mm
450 mm

questions.stem: A table in a manual gives values for '30 °C ambient'. What does 'ambient' mean here?
options: The temperature inside the cable's copper
The temperature of the air around it
The temperature of the water in the tank
The highest temperature the cable can take

questions.stem: For the same load, why does a long cable run often need a bigger cable than a short run?
options: To make the cable easier to pull through
To make the cable look stronger on the wall
To keep the voltage drop within the limit
To use up spare cable left from other jobs

questions.stem: The job specification asks for a higher standard than the code requires. What should you do?
options: Follow only the code, because the code is the law
Do whichever of the two is cheaper for the client
Ignore both and do what you did on the last job
Follow the specification, as it meets the code too

questions.stem: The specification asks for something that falls below what the code requires. What should you do?
options: Stop and report it, as the code minimum must be met
Follow the specification, as the client is paying
Do half of what each one of the two documents asks for
Follow it, but leave out the earth to save money

questions.stem: The drawing and the specification give different cable sizes for the same circuit. What should you do?
options: Use the smaller size, as it is easier to pull
Ask the designer to confirm it in writing
Use whichever size is already in the store
Toss a coin and note the result in the diary

questions.stem: Why must you follow the maker's installation instructions?
options: So the product looks the same as in the shop
So the job can be finished in the least time
So it is safe and its warranty stays valid
So the maker can charge the client more money

questions.stem: You want to fit a different make of breaker from the one named in the specification. What must you do first?
options: Fit it, as all breakers are the same inside
Fit it, and then tell the client after the job ends
Fit it only if it costs less than the other
Get approval for the change before fitting it

questions.stem: An instruction in a manual is not clear to you. What is the best action?
options: Ask your supervisor before you go on
Guess what it most likely means and carry on
Skip that step and do the next one
Do it the way you think is quickest

questions.stem: Where would you usually find the steps for making a machine safe before maintenance?
options: In the sales leaflet and the price list
In the delivery note from the supplier
In the manual and the site procedure
On the back of the machine's packing box

questions.stem: The drawing on site is 'Rev B', but the office says 'Rev D' has now been issued. What should you do?
options: Carry on with Rev B, as it is nearly the same
Stop using Rev B and get a copy of Rev D
Use Rev B for the morning and Rev D after lunch
Ask a trainee which one they would rather use

questions.stem: What should be done with an old (superseded) copy of a drawing on site?
options: Keep it with the new one, in case it is needed
Give it to the trainees to work from
Use the back of it for notes and sketches
Mark it 'superseded' or remove it from use

questions.stem: With approval, you change a cable route on site. What must happen to the drawings?
options: The change is marked on them for the record
Nothing, as the work is already finished
They are thrown away and new ones are not made
The change is only told to the next shift by word

questions.stem: Why should the manuals for installed equipment be handed to the client at the end of a job?
options: So the client can sell them to another company
So the electrician has less paper to carry
So it is used and looked after correctly
So the client knows the price of each item

questions.stem: Before you service a piece of equipment, which part of its manual should you read first?
options: The list of spare parts and their prices
The safety warnings and isolation steps
The history of the company that made it
The pages showing the colours available

questions.stem: Before working on an installation, what does safe isolation mean?
options: Switch off at the switch, then start the work straight away
Take out the fuse, put it in your pocket and start the work
Switch off and ask a friend to stand by the switch for you
Switch off, lock, tag and prove dead with a checked tester

questions.stem: A manual says a drive must be left for 5 minutes after switching off before its cover is removed. Why?
options: To let its capacitors lose their stored charge
To let the cooling fan blow the dust out first
To let the display show the last fault code
To let the room cool down for the electrician

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: In a specification, which word means that a requirement MUST be done: 'shall' or 'should'?
What do the letters RCD stand for?
On equipment marked IP65, what do the letters IP stand for?
What is the frequency of the mains supply in Jamaica, in hertz (Hz)?
What is the name for the part at the back of a standard or manual that holds extra tables and information?
What is the name of the list of words and their meanings that is often found in a manual or standard?
What is the name for drawings that have been corrected to show the work as it was actually installed?
A drawing has a scale of 1:50. A wall measures 80 mm on the drawing. How long is the real wall, in metres?
What does the prefix 'mega' (M), as in MΩ, mean?
Which signal word on a safety label is used for a hazard that WILL cause death or serious injury if it is not avoided?
What is the name for an official change or addition published to a standard after it was first issued?
On a motor nameplate, the duty is shown as S1. What type of duty is this?
What tool is used to tighten a terminal screw to the exact value given in the maker's instructions?
What is the name of the part of a drawing that explains what each symbol means?
When the drawings or specification are unclear, a written question is sent to the designer. What is this called? (You may give the letters.)

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a code (regulations), a standard, a job specification and a maker's manual. Give an example of what each one tells an electrician.
essays.modelAnswer: A code, or set of regulations, is a set of rules that is made law. Every installation must meet it, and it sets the minimum for safety, for example the protection a circuit must have. An inspector checks the work against it. A standard is an agreed document on how a product should be made or tested, or how a job should be done, for example how a cable must be built and tested. Codes often point to standards. A job specification is written for one job by the client or the designer. It says exactly what is wanted, for example the type of light fittings, the cable sizes, the finish and the makes allowed. It may ask for more than the code, but never for less. A maker's manual comes with one product and tells you how to install, use and maintain it, for example the clear spaces, the terminal connections and the service checks.
markingPoints: Code or regulations: rules made law, the minimum every installation must meet, with an example
Standard: an agreed way to make, test or do something, with an example
Specification: written for one job, says what the client wants; may ask for more than the code, not less
Maker's manual: how to install, use and maintain one product, with an example
The four are clearly compared, not just listed

essays.stem: Describe how you would find a piece of information quickly in a large manual or standard, and how you would make sure it is the right information.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check that I have the right document: the right product model or the right standard, and the latest edition or revision. Then I use the table of contents at the front to find the chapter or section that covers my topic, such as installation or earthing. If I am looking for one word or item, I use the index at the back, which lists topics in alphabetical order with page numbers. I use the section numbers, such as 5.3, to move around, and I follow any cross-references, such as 'see Table 4'. If I meet a word I do not know, I look it up in the glossary or definitions. Extra tables are often in an appendix. Once I find the information, I read the whole section, including the notes and warnings, not just one line, and I check the units. If it is still unclear, I ask my supervisor.
markingPoints: Checks it is the right document and the latest edition or revision
Uses the table of contents to find the right chapter
Uses the index for a single word or item
Uses section numbers, cross-references, the glossary and appendices
Reads the whole section with notes, warnings and units; asks if unclear

essays.stem: Explain what you should do if the drawing, the specification, the maker's instructions and the code do not agree with each other.
essays.modelAnswer: I must not guess or simply choose the easiest option. First I stop that part of the work and note exactly where the documents disagree, with the page, clause or drawing number. The code sets the legal minimum, so nothing may be done below it. If the specification asks for more than the code, the specification is followed, as it still meets the code. If the specification asks for less, it must be raised, because the code still has to be met. The maker's instructions must also be followed, as the product is only approved and under warranty when it is installed as the maker says. Where a drawing and a specification disagree, I do not decide myself. I report it to my supervisor, who sends a written question to the designer or engineer. I wait for a written answer before carrying on, and I keep that answer with the job records so the drawings can be updated.
markingPoints: Stops, does not guess, and notes exactly where the documents disagree
The code is the legal minimum: nothing may be done below it
A specification that asks for more is followed; one that asks for less is raised
The maker's instructions are followed (approval and warranty)
Reports to the supervisor, gets a written answer and keeps it with the records

essays.stem: Describe the information found on a motor nameplate, and explain how you would use it when planning the installation.
essays.modelAnswer: A motor nameplate gives the maker's ratings. The rated voltage tells me what supply it needs; if two voltages are shown, the terminals must be linked to suit the supply. The number of phases and the frequency must match the supply, which in Jamaica is 50 Hz. The power in kW is the output at the shaft at full load. The rated current at full load helps me choose the cable, the protective device and the overload setting, together with the maker's tables and the code. The speed in rpm tells me whether it suits the driven machine. The insulation class shows the highest temperature the windings can take, and the IP rating shows the protection against dust and water, so I can check that it suits the location, such as outdoors. The duty, such as S1 for continuous running, and the frame size, which helps with the base and fixings, are also shown. I check each item against the job before the motor is fitted.
markingPoints: Voltage, phases and frequency (50 Hz in Jamaica) must match the supply; dual voltage linked to suit
Rated current used to choose the cable, protective device and overload setting
Power (kW at the shaft) and speed (rpm) must suit the driven machine
IP rating and insulation class must suit the location and conditions
Other items (duty, frame size) noted and everything checked before fitting

essays.stem: Explain why you must follow the maker's installation instructions, and give four examples of things those instructions tell you.
essays.modelAnswer: The maker has designed and tested the product to work safely when it is installed in a certain way. If I do not follow the instructions, the product may overheat, fail early, give someone a shock or start a fire. The product's approval and the maker's warranty usually only apply when the instructions are followed, so a wrong installation can leave the client with no cover, and the inspector may fail the work. Examples of what the instructions tell me are: the supply voltage, current and frequency needed; the size of cable and the rating of the protective device; the clear space to leave around the product for cooling and for service; the mounting position and fixings; how to connect the terminals and the tightening value for each screw; the earthing connection; and the checks to make before the product is switched on by an authorised person. I keep the manual and hand it to the client at the end of the job.
markingPoints: Safety: the product is designed and tested to be safe only when installed as the maker says
Approval and warranty depend on it; the inspector may fail the work
Two correct examples (such as supply, cable and protective device, clear spaces)
Two more correct examples (such as mounting, terminals and tightening, earthing, checks)
Keeps the manual and hands it to the client

essays.stem: Explain what the two digits of an IP rating mean, and say how you would choose the IP rating for a light fitting on the outside wall of a house in Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: An IP rating is written as the letters IP and two digits, such as IP65. The first digit shows how well the enclosure keeps out solid objects and dust, from 0 (no protection) up to 6 (dust-tight). The second digit shows how well it keeps out water, from 0 (no protection) upwards: for example 4 means splashing water, 5 means water jets, and the highest numbers are for being put under water. The higher the digit, the better the protection. An X, as in IPX4, means that digit was not tested. On the outside wall of a house in Jamaica, the fitting will get heavy rain blown sideways, dust, and perhaps water from a hose, so it needs good protection against both. I would check the specification and the maker's data, and choose a rating such as IP65 or higher, or what the specification asks for. It must also be fitted the way up the maker says, with the right seals and glands, or the rating is lost.
markingPoints: First digit: protection against solids and dust (6 = dust-tight)
Second digit: protection against water, with a correct example
Higher digits give more protection; X means not tested
Outdoor conditions in Jamaica: driving rain, dust, hosing
Chooses a suitable rating (such as IP65) from the specification and maker's data, and fits it correctly

essays.stem: Explain why only the latest revision of a drawing or document must be used on a job, and how you would make sure you have it.
essays.modelAnswer: Drawings and documents are often changed during a job: the client may add a socket, the designer may change a cable size, or a standard may be updated. Each change is given a new revision letter or number and a date. If someone works from an old copy, work may be done wrongly and have to be taken out, materials may be wasted, and the installation may not be safe or may not meet the code. To make sure I have the latest one, I check the revision and date in the title block against the drawing register or issue list from the office, or I ask the supervisor. I check the edition date of standards and manuals in the same way. When a new revision arrives, the old copy is marked 'superseded' and removed from the work area, so that nobody picks it up by mistake. I read the revision notes so that I know what has changed.
markingPoints: Documents change during a job and each change gets a new revision and date
Working from an old copy causes wrong work, waste, or unsafe or non-compliant work
Checks the revision and date against the register or with the supervisor
Checks the editions of standards and manuals too
Old copies are marked superseded or removed; revision notes are read

essays.stem: Explain how to use a maker's cable rating table to choose a cable size, including what you must do when the cable runs in a hot place or is bunched with other cables.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the current the circuit must carry, from the load's rating or the design, and the rating of the protective device. Then I find the right table for the cable type and for the way it is installed, such as in conduit, clipped to a wall or in trunking, because each method has its own column. I read down the column to find the smallest cable whose rating is at least the current needed. The table ratings are for a set air temperature and for a cable on its own. If the cable runs through a hot place, such as a roof space in the Jamaican sun, or is bunched with other cables, it cannot get rid of its heat so well. So I apply the correction factors given with the table, which lower the cable's rating, and check again that the chosen size is still big enough; if it is not, I choose the next size up. For long runs I also check the voltage drop. I ask my supervisor to check my choice.
markingPoints: Finds the current the circuit must carry and the protective device rating
Uses the right table and column for the cable type and installation method
Chooses the smallest cable whose rating is at least the current needed
Heat and bunching lower the rating: applies the correction factors and re-checks, going up a size if needed
Checks voltage drop on long runs and has the choice checked

essays.stem: Describe the safety information you can find in makers' manuals and in safety data sheets, and explain how you use it before starting work.
essays.modelAnswer: Makers' manuals have a safety section near the front, with warnings marked by signal words such as DANGER, WARNING and CAUTION, and by symbols. They tell me the hazards of the equipment, such as high voltage, stored energy in capacitors, hot parts or moving parts, and how to isolate it safely, how long to wait after switching off, and what PPE to wear. A safety data sheet comes with a chemical, such as pipe cement, a cleaner or cable-pulling lubricant. It tells me the hazards, safe handling and storage, the ventilation and PPE needed, what to do if there is a spill or a fire, and first aid if it gets on the skin or in the eyes, or is breathed in. Before work I read these sections, check that the PPE and first-aid items are ready, and include the hazards in my job safety plan. I isolate as the manual says: switch off, lock off and tag, then prove dead with a tester checked before and after use.
markingPoints: Manuals: safety warnings and signal words, and the hazards of the equipment
Manuals: isolation steps, waiting times for stored energy, PPE
Safety data sheets: hazards, handling, storage, ventilation and PPE
Safety data sheets: spills, fire and first aid
Reads them before work, prepares PPE and first aid, and isolates safely as instructed

essays.stem: Explain why changes made on site must be recorded on the drawings and in the job records, and describe what you would record.
essays.modelAnswer: Records must show what was really installed. If a cable route, a circuit or the position of a box is changed on site, the next electrician, the inspector and the client need to know, or someone may drill into a hidden cable, isolate the wrong circuit or order the wrong parts. Up-to-date records also help with fault-finding and with adding to the installation later. When a change is made, with approval, I mark it on the site copy of the drawing in a clear colour, with the date and my initials, and tell the supervisor so that the office can update the drawing and issue a new revision. At the end of the job these marked-up copies become the as-built drawings. In the job records I note what was changed and why, who approved it, the materials used, and the test results for the circuits. I keep the makers' manuals and warranty papers with the records and hand them to the client.
markingPoints: Records must show what was really installed, for the safety of others (hidden cables, wrong circuit)
Records help with later fault-finding and additions
Marks changes on the site drawing with date and initials, and tells the supervisor
Marked-up drawings become the as-built drawings
Job records: what changed and why, approval, materials, test results; manuals handed over

practical1.title: Prepare an installation information sheet from a nameplate and a maker's manual
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a piece of workshop equipment (for example an exhaust fan, a water pump, a small motor or an inverter) with its maker's manual, a copy of a cable rating table and the Centre's blank information sheet. The equipment is not connected to any supply. As a group, find and record everything needed to plan its installation: the nameplate ratings (voltage, phases, frequency, power, current, IP rating and any other markings), the supply needed, the cable size from the table (with any correction for heat), the protective device the maker asks for, the clear spaces and mounting position, the earthing, the terminal connections and tightening values, the safety warnings and isolation steps, and the maintenance checks. Each member is given one or two sections to find, writes them on the sheet with the page or table number where they found them, and then explains their part to the group and the assessor. Together, check the sheet against the manual and list any questions for the supervisor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: One piece of workshop equipment with a readable nameplate, not connected to any supply
The maker's manual for that equipment
A copy of a cable rating table with its correction factors
The Centre's blank installation information sheet
Highlighters, sticky notes, pens and a calculator
photos: The equipment's nameplate, close up and readable
The group with the manual open at the contents or index page
The sticky notes or highlights marking the pages each member used
The cable table with the chosen row and column highlighted
The completed information sheet, with page references
Each member explaining their section to the assessor
checklist: Read the nameplate correctly and recorded every rating with its units
Used the contents, index and section numbers to find information quickly
Recorded the page, section or table number for every item found
Chose the cable size from the table correctly and applied any correction
Found and recorded the safety warnings and the isolation steps
Checked that the equipment's ratings match the supply, including 50 Hz
Explained their own section clearly and correctly to the assessor
Listed sensible questions for the supervisor where the documents were unclear
safety: The equipment stays disconnected from any supply for the whole task
Lift heavy equipment with help, using a correct lift, and keep it on a stable bench
Do not open any cover unless the instructor allows it and has made the equipment safe
Keep the work area tidy and bags off the floor

practical2.title: Read a job specification and drawing, and prepare a materials list and a query sheet
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a job pack for a small installation, such as a classroom with lights, switches, sockets and an exhaust fan: a layout drawing to scale, a short job specification and a page of extracts from a code or standard. Some details in the pack disagree on purpose. As a group: (1) highlight every item on the drawing and count each type, using the symbols explained on the drawing; (2) list the requirements in the specification, such as cable type and sizes, fittings, mounting heights, IP ratings, makes allowed and tests; (3) make a materials list with quantities, measuring the cable runs from the drawing with a scale rule; (4) find each place where the drawing, the specification and the code extract disagree, and write a query sheet for the supervisor, saying where each problem is and what needs to be decided. Each member leads one part, every member works on at least two parts, and each member signs the parts they did. Present the finished materials list and query sheet to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Job pack: layout drawing to scale, short job specification, and code or standard extracts
Scale rule, highlighters in different colours and pens
Blank materials list and query sheet forms
photos: The job pack laid out at the start
The drawing with each type of item highlighted and counted
The specification with the requirements marked
A member measuring a cable run with the scale rule
The completed materials list with quantities
The completed query sheet, signed by the members
checklist: Identified each symbol on the drawing correctly
Counted the items on the drawing correctly
Picked out the key requirements from the specification
Measured cable runs correctly using the drawing scale
Found the places where the documents disagree
Wrote clear queries saying where each problem is and what must be decided
Did not settle a conflict by guessing; raised it on the query sheet
Worked as part of the team and signed the parts they did
safety: Keep the work area tidy so that nobody trips over bags or chairs
Use the scale rule and any cutting tools carefully
If the task moves into the workshop, follow the Centre's rules there and wear the PPE required
Take short breaks during long spells of reading and writing
